result:
Neither five nor ten: **more agents don't always give better results.** Start with one.

Say a student asks, "Is the laser cutter free Friday, and do I need training?" With a calendar agent, a manual agent and a training agent, something has to pass the question around and combine the replies. Each handoff can lose details and adds **tokens** (the chunks of text a model reads and writes, which usage is typically billed by). One agent with a few tools keeps it all in one place.

The idea is tempting because extra agents can help. In Anthropic's [research system test](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system), several agents beat one by 90.2% on its internal research evaluation. But they suited questions with independent lines of search, and used about 15 times the tokens of a chat (not of one agent).

A [later Claude article](https://claude.com/resources/articles/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them) reports 3–10 times the tokens of one agent for equivalent tasks. It names three main reasons to split:
- **Cluttered context:** one subtask piles up mostly irrelevant text in what the model reads, hurting other work.
- **Parallel work:** independent parts can be explored separately.
- **Specialization:** one agent struggles with too many tools or conflicting roles.

**Next step:** build one agent, test it on real student questions, and split only if failures or measurements show one of these needs. With your small budget, that's easy to defend at design review.

Your turn: a teammate proposes a separate booking agent "because booking is a different job." What evidence would you ask for? I can also make this a short lesson.
